questions.question: What is @RestController in Spring Boot?
questions.title: @RestController annotation explained
questions.direct_answer: @RestController is a combination of @Controller and @ResponseBody. @Controller marks a class as a Spring MVC controller. @ResponseBody tells Spring to write the return value directly to the HTTP response body (as JSON by default) instead of looking for a view template. @RestController saves you from adding @ResponseBody to every method.
questions.interviewer_intent: One of the most common Spring Boot interview questions — verify the candidate knows what the annotation does.

sections.content: Think of @RestController as a convenience shortcut. Before it existed in Spring 4, if you were building a REST API you'd put @Controller on the class and @ResponseBody on every method. @ResponseBody is the key piece — it tells Spring 'don't look for a JSP or Thymeleaf template, just serialize this object to JSON and write it to the response.' @RestController combines both into one annotation at the class level. That's all it does. Behind the scenes, Jackson converts your returned objects to JSON automatically.
@RestController = @Controller + @ResponseBody. Return objects become JSON automatically via Jackson.

questions.question: What is the difference between @GetMapping, @PostMapping, @PutMapping, @DeleteMapping?
questions.title: HTTP method mapping annotations in Spring Boot
questions.direct_answer: @GetMapping maps GET requests (read). @PostMapping maps POST requests (create). @PutMapping maps PUT requests (replace/update). @DeleteMapping maps DELETE requests (delete). All are shortcuts for @RequestMapping(method = RequestMethod.GET/POST/etc.). Use the specific annotations — they communicate intent and are shorter.
questions.interviewer_intent: Basic REST API knowledge — verify the candidate maps HTTP verbs to CRUD operations.

sections.content: These are composed annotations — each one is @RequestMapping with a specific HTTP method pre-set. The reason they exist is readability: @GetMapping('/users') is much clearer than @RequestMapping(value='/users', method=RequestMethod.GET). In REST API design, the convention is: GET for reading data, POST for creating new resources, PUT for replacing an existing resource, DELETE for removing. PATCH is for partial updates. There's also @PatchMapping. Use these specific annotations consistently — they make your API's intent obvious.
All four are shortcuts for @RequestMapping with a specific method. Always prefer the specific annotation.

questions.question: What is the difference between @PathVariable and @RequestParam?
questions.title: @PathVariable vs @RequestParam in Spring Boot
questions.direct_answer: @PathVariable extracts a value from the URL path segment: /users/{id} → @PathVariable Long id. @RequestParam extracts a value from the query string: /users?status=active → @RequestParam String status. Path variables identify a resource; query parameters filter or modify the request.
questions.interviewer_intent: Extremely common question — verify the candidate knows both annotations and when to use each.

sections.content: The difference is where in the URL the value comes from. @PathVariable reads from the path itself — the curly brace placeholder in the URL pattern. So /users/42 maps to @PathVariable Long id = 42. Path variables are used to identify a specific resource. @RequestParam reads from the query string — the part after the question mark. So /users?status=active&page=2 gives you @RequestParam String status = 'active'. Query params are used for filtering, sorting, pagination. A good mental model: path variable = which resource, query param = how to filter or shape the response.

questions.question: What is @RequestBody and how does it work?
questions.title: @RequestBody in Spring Boot REST controllers
questions.direct_answer: @RequestBody tells Spring to read the HTTP request body and deserialize it into a Java object using Jackson. It is used with POST, PUT, and PATCH methods that send JSON in the request body. Jackson automatically maps JSON field names to Java field names.
questions.interviewer_intent: Core REST API building block — verify the candidate knows how POST request bodies are handled.

sections.content: When a client sends a POST request with a JSON body, Spring needs to turn that JSON string into a Java object. @RequestBody triggers that conversion. Jackson reads the JSON, looks at the field names, and maps them to the corresponding Java object fields. If the client sends {"name": "Alice", "email": "alice@example.com"}, Jackson creates a CreateUserRequest object with those fields set. If Jackson can't deserialize the JSON — wrong format, missing required field — it throws an HttpMessageNotReadableException and Spring returns a 400. Combined with @Valid, you get both format checking and constraint checking.
@RequestBody = Jackson deserializes JSON to Java object. Combine with @Valid for input validation.

questions.question: How do you return different HTTP status codes in Spring Boot?
questions.title: HTTP status codes in Spring Boot — ResponseEntity and @ResponseStatus
questions.direct_answer: Two approaches: @ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.CREATED) on a method sets a fixed status code. ResponseEntity<T> as the return type lets you set status, headers, and body dynamically — useful when the status depends on the result. ResponseEntity is more flexible; @ResponseStatus is simpler for fixed codes.
questions.interviewer_intent: Proper HTTP status codes matter for REST API design — verify the candidate knows how to control them.

sections.content: By default, Spring returns 200 OK for successful methods. But good REST APIs are more precise. A POST that creates a resource should return 201 Created. A successful DELETE with no body should return 204 No Content. For fixed status codes, just add @ResponseStatus to the method. For dynamic cases — like returning 200 if found, or 404 if not — use ResponseEntity as your return type and build it with ResponseEntity.ok(user) or ResponseEntity.notFound().build(). ResponseEntity is the most expressive option.
ResponseEntity for dynamic status codes. @ResponseStatus for fixed codes. ResponseEntity is more flexible.

questions.question: What is @ControllerAdvice and how do you handle exceptions globally in Spring Boot?
questions.title: @ControllerAdvice for global exception handling
questions.direct_answer: @ControllerAdvice combined with @ExceptionHandler lets you handle exceptions across all controllers in one place. Without it, every controller method would need its own try-catch. @ControllerAdvice is an interceptor that catches specified exceptions and maps them to HTTP responses — for example catching ResourceNotFoundException and returning 404.
questions.interviewer_intent: Exception handling is a real-world concern — tests whether the candidate goes beyond basic CRUD controllers.

sections.content: Without global exception handling, every controller method needs to catch exceptions and convert them to error responses. That's repetitive and inconsistent. @ControllerAdvice centralizes this. You create one class, annotate it, and define @ExceptionHandler methods. Each handler method catches a specific exception type and returns an appropriate response. So when any controller throws a ResourceNotFoundException, your handler catches it and returns a 404 with a structured error body — same format across all endpoints. This is how you build consistent error responses in a Spring Boot app.
@RestControllerAdvice = @ControllerAdvice + @ResponseBody. Use it for a central error-handling class.

questions.question: What is @RequestMapping at the class level used for?
questions.title: @RequestMapping class-level base path
questions.direct_answer: @RequestMapping on a controller class sets a base path prefix for all methods in that class. If the class has @RequestMapping("/users") and a method has @GetMapping("/{id}"), the full path is /users/{id}. This avoids repeating the base path on every method and groups related endpoints.
questions.interviewer_intent: Basic Spring MVC knowledge — verify the candidate understands URL composition from class + method levels.

sections.content: Putting @RequestMapping on the class sets a root path for all the methods inside. Without it, you'd have to write /users/ in every @GetMapping, @PostMapping, etc. With it on the class, all the method-level mappings are relative paths that get combined. @GetMapping('/{id}') on a class with @RequestMapping('/users') becomes GET /users/{id}. This is the standard way to group endpoints — one controller, one resource, one class-level @RequestMapping.
Class-level @RequestMapping = base URL. Method-level mapping = relative path. Final URL = base + method path.
